lines.t: His ship sank in two minutes. He had a tiny wooden raft, food for about fifty days... and he would need one hundred and thirty-three.
He was the ship's steward. Middle of the Atlantic. And he couldn't really swim.
So he tied a rope from the raft to his wrist. Every single day.
The food ran out after fifty-five days. The water, about fifteen days later.
So he got creative. He pulled a nail out of the raft... and bent it into a fishing hook.
Rope became fishing line. Biscuit crumbs became bait.
Little fish caught bigger fish. Rain filled his life jacket. Seagulls landed... and became dinner.
One day a ship passed. Close. He waved. He screamed. It kept going.
Then a plane flew over! It dropped a marker... and a storm blew him away from it.
Then he hooked a shark. And the shark fought back. Right there, on the raft.
He won with the water jug. And the shark's liver became something to drink.
You see, out there, the deadline is water, not food. So every single thing on that raft became a tool. The nail. The rope. The jug. The jacket.
On day one hundred and thirty-three, three fishermen found him near Brazil. He had drifted over a thousand kilometers.
When they told him nobody had ever survived that long on a raft, he said...
I hope no one ever has to break that record.
Day one on that raft. What do you save first? A, the food. Or B, the rope.
